strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean generalization of Diffusion DPO that moves supervision from final-sample preferences to per-timestep denoising transition preferences, with a careful derivation (including full appendix proofs) connecting the new objective back to Diffusion DPO and DSPO as special cases.

Proposes a practical, label-free instantiation using prompt perturbation with a frozen reference model, removing the need for costly human preference annotations or trained reward models, which is a meaningful practical contribution for scalability.

Very broad empirical validation: controlled 2D toy experiments illustrating the core mechanism, real text-to-image alignment (GenEval, T2I-CompBench) and aesthetic-quality experiments (HPSv2, PickScore) on three different backbones (SD-1.4, SDXL, and the flow-matching SANA), plus FID/IS quality checks.

Comparisons against multiple strong, differently-supervised baselines (Diffusion DPO, DSPO, SPO, D-KTO, MAPO, IterComp, CaPO) show DDSPO is competitive or superior despite using no human-labeled data or reward models.

Thorough ablations: dataset-size scaling, β sensitivity, different perturbation strategies (random removal vs. LLM-based), and an 'efficient' variant that avoids generating explicit negative images, together with reasonably detailed reproducibility information (training configs, prompts, schedulers) in the supplement.
Qualitative results across alignment and aesthetic settings support the quantitative claims and provide intuitive illustration of improvements.
weaknesses: The practical instantiation largely reduces to reference-model self-distillation plus a contrastive repulsion term from a degraded-prompt output (as the paper itself notes the 'winning' term simplifies to standard distillation loss); this weakens the claim that genuine stepwise 'preference' signal is being learned beyond a heuristic contrastive regularizer, and the framing as a rigorous instantiation of the general policy-pair theory is not strongly justified beyond intuition.

The general DDSPO formulation (with true accessible winning/losing policies) is validated only in a small, somewhat constructed 2D toy setting where 'losing' samples are simply neighboring-class samples; no real-data experiment demonstrates the general formulation with actual labeled preference pairs, so the paper's strongest claims rest almost entirely on the heuristic prompt-perturbation instantiation.

Because the reference model used for supervision is the same pretrained backbone being fine-tuned, the method's gains are bounded by what can be achieved via repulsion from degraded-prompt conditioning rather than any external stronger signal; this should be discussed more explicitly as it affects the interpretation of 'preference optimization' versus contrastive self-distillation.

Only 100 training iterations are used in main experiments, which is unusually small; it is unclear whether baseline methods (D-DPO, DSPO, SPO, etc.) are given equivalent optimization budgets/tuning for fair comparison, raising some reproducibility and fairness concerns.

Evaluation relies exclusively on automated metrics (GenEval, T2I-CompBench, HPSv2, PickScore, FID/IS); no human study is conducted to validate perceived alignment or aesthetic improvements, which is a common limitation but still relevant given the paper's emphasis on human-preference alignment.

Performance is mixed relative to SOTA baselines that do use labeled data (e.g., SPO clearly outperforms DDSPO on aesthetic metrics for SDXL, and IterComp/CaPO occasionally win on individual GenEval/CompBench sub-metrics), so claims of matching or surpassing existing methods should be read as approximately comparable rather than uniformly superior.
The cost of constructing the pseudo-preference dataset (~5 H100-days for 200K pairs) is non-trivial and should be weighed against the claimed efficiency advantage over label-based approaches.

strengths: The paper provides a fairly complete theoretical derivation connecting DPO, Diffusion DPO, and the proposed DDSPO objective, including a clear discussion of how Diffusion DPO can be viewed as a special case of DDSPO and how DSPO can be reformulated with the proposed 'contrastive policy pair' (CPP) signal.

The practical instantiation avoids costly human-labeled preference datasets and reward models by using prompt perturbation with a frozen reference model, which is an appealing and scalable idea for the preference-optimization literature.

Experiments are extensive: a controlled 2D toy setting isolating the core mechanism, three diffusion/flow-matching backbones (SD-1.4, SDXL, SANA), two alignment benchmarks (GenEval, T2I-CompBench), two aesthetic benchmarks (HPSv2, PickScore), FID/IS for fidelity, and multiple ablations (dataset size, β sweep, perturbation strategy, efficient positive-only variant).

Comparisons include a reasonably broad set of baselines (Diffusion DPO, DSPO, SPO, D-KTO, MAPO, IterComp, CaPO), and the supplementary material offers detailed derivations, implementation details, and generous qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The claimed advantage of DDSPO over DSPO (i.e., true stepwise, policy-grounded supervision vs. forward-process-approximated supervision) is undercut by the paper's own ablation: 'DSPO+CPP' (DSPO simply augmented with the same contrastive-policy-pair signal) matches or slightly exceeds DDSPO on CompBench (.3854 vs .3823) and is close on other metrics, suggesting that most of the empirical gain comes from the prompt-perturbation/CPP trick itself rather than from the specific stepwise DPO reformulation that is presented as the paper's main theoretical contribution.

In practice, the 'contrastive policy pair' is instantiated only as the same frozen reference model conditioned on the original prompt vs. a semantically/aesthetically degraded prompt; this reduces to a distillation-plus-repulsion signal in noise space that is conceptually close to existing negative-prompting/CFG-style techniques, but this relationship is not discussed or contrasted, making the degree of genuine novelty harder to assess.

Reported comparisons to SOTA are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: on aesthetic quality (Table 4), DDSPO is consistently below SPO on both SD-1.5 and SDXL (e.g., HPSv2 28.78 vs 29.21, PickScore 22.70 vs 23.11 on SDXL), and on GenEval sub-metrics (Table A) DDSPO trails IterComp on Counting, Color Attribution, and CaPO/IterComp on some T2I-CompBench sub-categories (Spatial, Non-Spatial), which is understated in the main text's framing of 'outperforming or matching.'

All evaluation relies on automatic proxy metrics (GenEval, T2I-CompBench, HPSv2, PickScore, FID, IS) with no human preference study and no reported variance/seeds, despite the paper's central claim being about aligning with 'nuanced user intent' and 'aesthetic quality,' concepts that are typically best validated with human judgments.

The core assumption that degraded/perturbed prompts reliably define a valid 'dispreferred' denoising direction is not directly validated (e.g., via a sanity check that reference outputs under c− are indeed rated worse); its validity is inferred only indirectly through downstream benchmark gains.

The efficient (positive-only) variant that avoids generating dispreferred images shows a non-trivial drop relative to the full method (GenEval .4866–.4891 vs .5045), which somewhat weakens the practicality claims made for this variant.
Preference-optimized models show increased FID relative to the base model (e.g., SD-1.4 FID 13.05 → 16.39 with DDSPO), indicating some loss of output diversity/fidelity that is not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical extension of Diffusion DPO to transition-level (stepwise) preference supervision in score space, with full derivations connecting to the Bradley-Terry/DPO framework provided both in the main text and supplementary material.

The proposed label-free construction of preference signals via prompt perturbation and a frozen reference model is a practical and scalable contribution that removes the need for costly human-annotated preference datasets or reward models, addressing a real bottleneck in the field.

Experimental evaluation is extensive: a controlled 2D toy experiment clarifies the core mechanism; the method is validated across three distinct architectures (SD-1.4, SDXL, and the DiT-based flow-matching model SANA), on two different tasks (text-image alignment and aesthetic quality), and compared against multiple strong preference-optimization baselines (Diffusion DPO, DSPO, SPO, IterComp, CaPO, D-KTO, MAPO).

The paper clearly situates DDSPO relative to prior stepwise methods (DSPO, SPO), and even demonstrates the generality of its contrastive-policy-pair idea by reformulating DSPO with it (DSPO+CPP), showing consistent gains, which strengthens the conceptual contribution beyond a single method.

Thorough ablations are provided (dataset size, β sensitivity, different perturbation strategies, an efficient variant avoiding explicit negative image generation), along with detailed implementation/reproducibility details and an honest limitations discussion.
Qualitative results are provided across multiple backbones and tasks, offering intuitive support for the quantitative gains.
weaknesses: In the practical instantiation (Eq. 5), the 'preferred' term reduces to a plain knowledge-distillation loss toward the reference model conditioned on the original prompt, since the ∥ϵref−ϵref∥² term vanishes; this weakens the conceptual novelty of the 'contrastive policy pair' framing, as the actual preferred signal is not derived from any distinctly better generative policy but is simply the reference model's own prediction.

The distinction drawn between Diffusion DPO ('final-sample supervision') and DDSPO ('stepwise supervision') could be articulated more carefully: standard diffusion DPO training already computes losses per sampled timestep t; the real difference lies in which targets are used at each timestep (forward-process posterior vs. contrastive-policy targets) rather than a difference in whether supervision is 'stepwise' at all, and this nuance might confuse readers.

Performance versus SOTA is mixed rather than uniformly superior: for aesthetic quality (Table 4), DDSPO underperforms SPO (a method that also needs no reward-labeled data reliance is different, but SPO does use Pick-a-Pic-trained reward model) on both HPSv2 and PickScore for SDXL, tempering the abstract's claim of 'outperforming or matching' methods.

The method still requires substantial, architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning (β values differ greatly across SD-1.4/SDXL vs. SANA), which the paper itself flags as a practical limitation reducing plug-and-play usability.

Evaluation of aesthetic quality relies solely on learned metrics (HPSv2, PickScore) without any human study, which could be susceptible to biases of the underlying preference models and doesn't fully substantiate qualitative superiority.

The efficient variant that reuses random positive images as pseudo-negatives (Sec. 3.3/4.4) is justified only empirically and heuristically; its theoretical grounding is weaker than the main DDSPO formulation, and its generality beyond the tested regime is unclear.
FID/IS is reported for the alignment experiments but not for the aesthetic-quality experiments, leaving open whether aesthetic fine-tuning trades off diversity or introduces artifacts.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated technical contribution: the paper cleanly identifies the mismatch in Diffusion DPO/DSPO between forward-process-approximated supervision targets and the model's actual backward denoising transitions, and proposes a principled stepwise contrastive-policy-pair (CPP) formulation to address it, with a full derivation connecting DDSPO to DPO, Diffusion DPO, DSPO and SPO in a unified framework (Sec. 3.4 and Appendix A).

Two complementary and practical instantiations are proposed: DD-CPP (learned winning/losing policies from labeled data) and TF-CPP (training-free, using only prompt perturbation and a pretrained reference model), which substantially broadens applicability, including to settings without any human-annotated preference data.

Extensive empirical validation: controlled 2D toy experiments isolating the mechanism, text-to-image alignment (GenEval, T2I-CompBench) and aesthetic-quality experiments (HPSv2, PickScore) across multiple architectures (SD-1.4/1.5, SDXL, SANA, SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Large, U-Net and DiT/flow-matching backbones), comparisons against strong SOTA baselines (IterComp, CaPO, SPO, D-KTO, MAPO, SoftREPA), human evaluation, dataset-size ablations, seed-variance analysis, computational-cost benchmarking, and a CFG-style baseline control to rule out a trivial explanation of the gains.

The ablation replacing the supervision target inside DSPO with CPP-derived targets (DSPO+CPP) isolates the contribution of the core idea from the specific DDSPO objective and shows consistent improvement, strengthening the causal claim that policy-pair, transition-level supervision (rather than terminal-sample forward approximation) drives the benefit.

The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity to β, added computational cost of maintaining a contrastive policy pair, and dependence on the quality of the constructed CPP), and provides substantial implementation detail and additional ablations in the appendix to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Despite claims of removing forward-process approximation, the practical DDSPO algorithm still samples x_t via the forward noising process and approximates the joint transition distribution (Eq. 27) in a manner structurally similar to Diffusion DPO's own approximation; the paper could more carefully qualify the extent to which the backward-transition mismatch is actually eliminated versus merely changing which noise/target is regressed against.

Gains are inconsistent across metrics/categories: DDSPO underperforms in some GenEval subcategories (e.g., Counting, Color Attribution) relative to IterComp/CaPO, and in the aesthetic-quality comparison (Table 3) D-KTO and SPO outperform DDSPO on some metrics, which is acknowledged but tempers the overall strength of the claims.

FID increases for all preference-optimization methods relative to the base model, and although DDSPO shows the smallest increase, this points to a persistent image-diversity/quality trade-off that is only partially explained by the DiffusionDB/MS-COCO domain shift.

Human evaluation is limited in scope (only 15 annotators, 30 prompts, and only for the DD-CPP variant on SDXL versus Diffusion DPO); the margin of preference is modest (e.g., 42.9% vs 36.0% overall), and TF-CPP—the more novel, data-free variant—is not validated with human judgments.

The core idea underlying TF-CPP (using a degraded/perturbed condition on a frozen reference model to generate a synthetic negative direction) is conceptually related to existing self-training/contrastive-degradation approaches cited in related work; the paper's novelty is primarily in reformulating this idea as per-timestep policy-pair supervision rather than in the degraded-conditioning mechanism itself, which is an incremental combination of known ingredients.

Some cross-table numerical inconsistencies (e.g., SDXL+DDSPO CompBench values differ between Table 2a and 2b) stem from different evaluation protocols (3-in-1 vs. BLIP-VQA-only Complex metric) that are explained only in the appendix; this should be made clearer in the main text to avoid confusion.

TF-CPP's pseudo-preference data generation and DDSPO training incur non-trivial extra compute (e.g., ~5 H100-days to generate 200K pseudo-pairs plus ~1 H100-day of training for the SDXL setting), which, while still less than full RLHF pipelines, is a practical cost not fully contextualized against simpler baselines' costs.

strengths: The paper is well organized, with a full derivation from the DPO Bradley-Terry framework through Diffusion DPO to DSPO and the proposed DDSPO, connecting the three methods within a common formalism (Sec. 3.4, Appendix A) that is pedagogically useful.

Two concrete, non-trivial instantiations of the 'contrastive policy pair' idea are proposed (DD-CPP with separately fine-tuned winning/losing models, and TF-CPP with prompt degradation applied to a frozen reference model), the latter of which removes the need for human preference annotation.

The empirical evaluation is broad: multiple backbones (SD-1.4/1.5, SDXL, SANA, SD3-Medium/Large), two tasks (alignment and aesthetics), several benchmarks (GenEval, T2I-CompBench, HPSv2, PickScore, FID/IS), a toy 2D experiment, ablations on dataset size, degradation strategy, and computational cost, plus a modest human study.

Comparisons against relevant recent baselines (Diffusion DPO, DSPO, SPO, IterComp, CaPO, SoftREPA, a CFG-style baseline) are included, along with an honest ablation (DSPO+CPP) that isolates the effect of the proposed contrastive-pair data construction from the proposed loss reformulation.
weaknesses: The central claim that DDSPO 'directly' supervises backward transitions without forward-process approximation is overstated: the practical objective (Eq. 4/27) still samples x_t via the forward process q(x_t|x_0) and only replaces the noise target with outputs of an auxiliary trained/reference policy; the forward process is not eliminated, only relocated, which is a more incremental change than the framing suggests.

The ablation in Table 1 shows that simply adding contrastive-policy-pair (CPP) data construction to the existing DSPO objective (DSPO+CPP) nearly matches or even beats full DDSPO on CompBench, suggesting that much of the empirical benefit comes from the TF-CPP data/prompt-degradation trick rather than from the proposed stepwise reformulation of the loss itself, which undercuts the paper's core methodological contribution.

TF-CPP is conceptually very close to classifier-free-guidance-style contrastive decoding (contrasting predictions under an original vs. degraded prompt from the same frozen reference model); while a CFG-style baseline is compared (Table G) and underperforms, the delta appears attributable mainly to the DPO-style sigmoid/relative weighting rather than to a fundamentally new source of supervision.

Empirical gains are mixed and sometimes marginal: in Table 2b DDSPO lags CaPO/IterComp on several GenEval/CompBench subcategories (counting, color attribution, spatial, complex); in Table 3 D-KTO and SPO outperform DDSPO on several aesthetic metrics; FID after DDSPO training remains substantially higher than baseline (16.4 vs 13.1), tempered only by a post-hoc domain-shift argument.

The human evaluation is small-scale (15 annotators, 30 prompts, 450 judgments) with high tie rates (up to 47.8%) and margins of a few percentage points, with no statistical significance testing, limiting the strength of the human-preference claim.

Novelty relative to prior self-training/contrastive approaches (e.g., degraded-counterpart self-training methods cited in Sec. 2, DSPO, SPO) is somewhat incremental; the paper's differentiation rests largely on using policy-derived rather than forward-approximated per-step targets, a distinction that is conceptually reasonable but not dramatically new given the already crowded space of diffusion preference-optimization variants.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing implementation link in the abstract ('Our implementation is available at:' with no URL provided), and several typographical/notational slips throughout the derivations (e.g., 'nerual net work' on p.21) suggest the manuscript was not fully proofread.

The toy 2D experiment (Fig. 1), while illustrative, uses a very simple multi-modal Gaussian setup and provides limited evidence of how the mechanism scales to the very high-dimensional, densely packed condition spaces of real text-to-image generation, despite being used as the primary intuition-building demonstration.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a concrete mismatch in Diffusion DPO (its stepwise target is derived from the forward-process posterior over terminal samples, not the model's actual backward transitions) and proposes a principled fix (DDSPO) that supervises directly in score space using a contrastive policy pair at each timestep.

Two complementary, practical instantiations are proposed: DD-CPP (learned winning/losing policies from labeled preference data) and TF-CPP (training-free, using a reference model with original vs. degraded prompts), the latter removing the need for reward models or human annotations, which is a meaningful practical contribution given the absence of public preference datasets for T2I alignment.

Thorough derivations connecting DDSPO to DPO, Diffusion DPO, DSPO, and SPO are provided in the appendix, clarifying how existing methods are special cases or approximations of the proposed formulation.

Broad and fairly rigorous experimental validation: toy 2D experiments isolating the core mechanism, text-to-image alignment and aesthetic-quality experiments across multiple architectures (SD-1.4/1.5, SDXL, SANA, SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Large, covering both U-Net and DiT/flow-matching backbones), several ablations (dataset size, degradation strategy, negative-image-free variant, β sweep), a human evaluation study, and a five-seed robustness check.

Reasonable limitations discussion (β sensitivity, computational overhead of stepwise supervision, dependency on quality of the contrastive pair construction), and comparisons against a sensible CFG-style baseline and SoftREPA to isolate the source of TF-CPP's benefit.
weaknesses: Some approximations remain despite the claim that DDSPO "removes reliance on the forward process": the joint transition distribution is still approximated via forward noising to obtain x_t before applying the contrastive policy pair (Eq. 27), so the method reduces but does not eliminate forward-process dependence.

Empirical gains are often modest, and the method is not uniformly superior: Table 3 shows D-KTO and SPO sometimes outperform DDSPO/TF-CPP on aesthetic metrics, and the human evaluation margin over Diffusion-DPO, while consistent, is relatively small (e.g., 42.9% vs 36.0% overall preference, with high tie rates for prompt alignment).

FID increases relative to the base model for all preference-optimization methods including DDSPO; although attributed mainly to training/evaluation domain shift, this still leaves some ambiguity about whether alignment gains come with a quality/diversity trade-off.

TF-CPP construction relies on heuristic prompt-degradation strategies (random token removal, LLM-based rewriting) whose effectiveness varies by task and requires empirical tuning (Table 4a, Table H), suggesting the method's benefit is somewhat sensitive to the choice of degradation heuristic rather than derived from a principled degradation model.

Comparisons to strong SOTA methods (IterComp, CaPO) are mixed at the sub-metric level (e.g., DDSPO trails in Counting/Color Attribution on GenEval and in Spatial/Complex on CompBench), which tempers the claim of general superiority even though DDSPO uses less supervision.

The theoretical justification for why stepwise policy-pair supervision is better than forward-process approximation rests mainly on an illustrative 2D toy example rather than a formal analysis of when/why the approximation gap in Diffusion DPO matters quantitatively.
